summary: Tractate Yoma daf 77a covers: Ezekiel's vision of the sun-worshippers, Michael's plea, and Gabriel's coals; whether refraining from bathing constitutes inui (affliction); deriving the affliction of going barefoot; deriving the affliction of withholding conjugal relations.

display.whats: Ezekiel's vision of the sun-worshippers; Michael pleads for the righteous; Gabriel's coals cool in transit; Gabriel is punished for a full report; Dubiel, the angel of Persia, and Gabriel's plea for Israel
display.hint: What does the Gemara's telling of Ezekiel's vision, Gabriel's coals, and the angel of Persia teach about judgment and restraint?
display.title: Ezekiel's Vision: Gabriel, the Coals, and the Angel of Persia

learning.ahaMoment: The aggada is not a digression: it pairs mercy with justice - the coals cooling en route show God tempering deserved punishment, and Gabriel's own punishment for reporting the destruction in full shows that even a faithful agent of judgment must not broadcast an outcome, only hint at it.
learning.memoryAnchor: The coals cooled in transit - punishment tempered even when deserved; Gabriel was struck for saying too much, not for doing too little.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why does the Gemara linger on Ezekiel's vision of the sun-worshippers and follow it through Gabriel's punishment and the angel of Persia?
learning.coreTension: Between the severity of the decreed punishment and its restraint in practice: the same passage that condemns the sinners tempers their punishment through the cooling coals, rewards the merit of Torah scholars' wives and Daniel, and yet punishes Gabriel himself for reporting the destruction too fully.
learning.coreMove: The aggada draws two lessons from the vision: the coals cooling as they passed from the cherub to Gabriel shows that God tempers punishment even when it is deserved, and Gabriel's own punishment for delivering a full report of the destruction shows that an agent of judgment should only hint at an outcome, never announce it in detail.

takeaway.text: A single vision text can carry two independent lessons at once: the coals cooling en route show that punishment can be tempered even when fully deserved, and Gabriel's own punishment for delivering a full report of the destruction establishes that an agent of judgment should only hint at an outcome, never announce it in detail.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may treat the angelic narrative as pure aggada with no argumentative payoff, missing that it makes concrete claims about restraint in judgment and the ethics of delivering a report.

argumentFlow.label: Ezekiel's vision of sun-worshippers
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Ezekiel sees twenty-five men between the porch and the altar with their backs to the Sanctuary, worshipping the sun toward the east. The Gemara reads 'their backs toward the Temple' as teaching that they openly degraded the Divine Presence, the verse using a euphemism for their conduct.

argumentFlow.label: Michael pleads, Gabriel is sent to scatter the coals
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: God tells the angel Michael that his nation has sinned; Michael asks that the good be spared, but God responds that He will burn even the good among them, since they failed to rebuke the wicked. God then orders Gabriel to take coals of fire from between the cherubs and scatter them over the city.

argumentFlow.label: Why the coals cooled in transit
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida teaches that had the coals not cooled as they passed from the cherub's hand to Gabriel's hand, no remnant of the Jewish people would have survived. The delay in handing over the coals tempered the severity of the punishment.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners assume the angelic narrative is a digression with no halachic bearing, just aggada about Ezekiel's vision.
misconceptions.correction: The passage is woven into the larger sugya on Yom Kippur afflictions and divine judgment, and the Gemara uses these stories about Gabriel, the coals, and the wives of Torah scholars to make pointed claims about reward, restraint in punishment, and merit.

visualizableElements.item: Ezekiel's vision of the sun-worshippers, Michael's plea, Gabriel's cooling coals, and the angel of Persia

quizSeeds.question: Why does the Gemara stress that the coals cooled as they passed from the cherub to Gabriel?
quizSeeds.answer: The cooling shows that the punishment was deliberately tempered. Had Gabriel taken the still-hot coals directly, the destruction would have been total; the delay in the handoff is what left a remnant of the Jewish people alive.

quizSeeds.question: Why was Gabriel punished even though he carried out the mission he was sent on?
quizSeeds.answer: Not for failing, but for reporting back in full detail. The principle is that an agent of destruction should only hint at the outcome, not announce its success, so Gabriel was struck for delivering an open report of the devastation.

display.whats: Whether refraining from bathing constitutes inui (affliction)
display.hint: The Gemara asks whether refraining from bathing constitutes inui (self-affliction) as required by the Torah.
display.title: Is Not Bathing a Real Affliction?

learning.ahaMoment: The Talmud has a theory of the body: it ranks human needs, and only genuine needs generate genuine inui when withheld.
learning.memoryAnchor: Inui requires real need - bathing must prove itself as need, not luxury, before its absence qualifies.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why would the Talmud need to ask whether refraining from bathing is a genuine affliction?
learning.coreTension: Between common sense (not bathing is obviously uncomfortable) and the technical halakhic requirement that 'inui' means deprivation of something the body genuinely requires, not merely something pleasant.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara distinguishes discomfort from halakhic inui: to count as an affliction on YK, an abstention must deprive the body of a genuine need, not just a comfort. The question is whether bathing rises to the level of genuine bodily need.

takeaway.text: The five YK afflictions are not merely discomforts but deprivations of genuine bodily needs; a practice must rise to the level of genuine need for its absence to count as inui.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume all discomfort automatically qualifies as affliction; the Gemara's precision about what 'inui' means is a necessary step in the legal analysis.

argumentFlow.label: Trying to prove bathing is affliction from David's flight
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara seeks a source that abstaining from bathing counts as affliction. It cites that David's men were 'hungry, weary, and thirsty': hunger from lack of bread, thirst from lack of water, and 'weary' apparently from lack of bathing. The Gemara objects that 'weary' might instead mean lack of wearing shoes, so the proof fails.

argumentFlow.label: Deriving bathing as affliction from 'on a weary soul'
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rav Yitzchak offers a better source: 'As cold water on a weary soul.' The Gemara considers that 'weary' might mean thirst, but rejects this: the verse says cold water 'on' a weary soul, not 'in' it. Water placed on the body, rather than drunk, points to bathing, establishing that withholding it is affliction.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners think the Gemara is debating whether bathing is pleasurable, treating the question as common sense.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara already assumes bathing is a comfort; what it is actually hunting for is a scriptural verse that the word 'inui' (affliction) encompasses going unwashed, which is why it parses prepositions like 'on' versus 'in' so closely.

quizSeeds.question: Why does the first attempt to prove that withholding bathing is affliction fail?
quizSeeds.answer: The verse calls David's men 'weary,' but the Gemara cannot show that 'weary' specifically means unwashed; it could just as well refer to being without shoes, so the word does not uniquely establish bathing as the missing comfort.

quizSeeds.question: How does the wording 'cold water on a weary soul' settle that bathing is the relevant affliction?
quizSeeds.answer: The preposition 'on' rather than 'in' is decisive. Water drunk would enter the soul; water 'on' the soul is applied externally, which is bathing, so the verse ties weariness to the lack of washing rather than thirst.

sugyot.finalRuling: The Gemara asks whether refraining from bathing constitutes inui (self-affliction) as required by the Torah.
prerequisiteKnowledge: Understanding of Yom Kippur halachic framework

display.whats: Rejecting David's barefoot ascent and Isaiah's barefoot walk as proofs; deriving the shoe affliction from Jeremiah
display.hint: Why do David's barefoot ascent of the Mount of Olives and Isaiah's barefoot walk both fail to prove that going without shoes is a Yom Kippur affliction, and which verse finally succeeds?
display.title: Deriving the Affliction of Going Barefoot

learning.ahaMoment: The Gemara insists on a verse where 'barefoot' cannot be softened into anything but literal bare feet; David's and Isaiah's verses both admit non-literal readings, so only Jeremiah's explicit warning against letting the foot 'come to be barefoot' survives as the source.
learning.memoryAnchor: David: maybe just no horse. Isaiah: maybe just patched shoes. Jeremiah: literally 'withhold your foot from being barefoot' - that one sticks.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why do the Gemara's first two proof-texts for the barefoot affliction fail, and what makes Jeremiah's verse succeed where they did not?
learning.coreTension: Between the availability of vivid narrative descriptions of people going barefoot and the need for a verse where 'barefoot' cannot be softened into a non-literal reading.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara tests two candidate verses and rejects both because 'barefoot' can be read non-literally there (a king stripped of his horse and whip, or patched shoes read like 'naked' meaning ragged clothing); only Jeremiah's verse, where bare feet are explicitly cast as a hardship to be withheld from, survives as the source.

takeaway.text: Going barefoot (without shoes) is a Yom Kippur affliction, derived not from narrative descriptions of barefoot walking (which can always be read non-literally) but from Jeremiah's explicit warning to withhold the foot from becoming barefoot, which casts bare feet unambiguously as a hardship to avoid.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume the first vivid image of someone walking barefoot settles the derivation; the Gemara instead requires a verse immune to a non-literal reading of 'barefoot.'

argumentFlow.label: Trying to prove going barefoot is affliction from David
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara asks for the source that not wearing shoes is an affliction, citing that David went up the Mount of Olives weeping, head covered, and barefoot. The proof is rejected: 'barefoot' might describe a king deprived of his horse and whip rather than literally lacking shoes.

argumentFlow.label: Isaiah's barefoot walk and the patched-shoes challenge
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites Isaiah, commanded to remove his shoe and who then walked 'naked and barefoot.' The Gemara objects that 'barefoot' might mean patched shoes, just as 'naked' must mean ragged garments rather than literally unclothed, so this verse also fails to prove the point.

argumentFlow.label: Deriving the shoe affliction from Jeremiah
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak gives the conclusive source from Jeremiah: 'Withhold your foot from being barefoot,' read homiletically as keeping oneself from sin so the foot does not come to be bare. The verse treats being barefoot as a hardship to be avoided, establishing that going without shoes is an affliction.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners expect the first verse showing someone barefoot to settle that going shoeless is an affliction.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara repeatedly rejects verses where 'barefoot' can be read non-literally (a king without his horse, patched shoes) and accepts only Jeremiah's verse, where being barefoot is plainly cast as a hardship to be withheld from.

quizSeeds.question: Why does the verse about David walking barefoot up the Mount of Olives fail as a source for the shoe affliction?
quizSeeds.answer: Because a king's 'barefoot' state could be metaphorical: a king stripped of his horse and whip was described as going barefoot even while wearing shoes, so the verse does not prove that literally lacking shoes is an affliction.

quizSeeds.question: How does the rejection of Isaiah's 'naked and barefoot' parallel the patched-shoes reading?
quizSeeds.answer: Just as 'naked' cannot be taken literally and must mean ragged clothing, 'barefoot' can be softened to mean patched shoes. The two terms are read consistently, so the verse loses its force as a literal proof about shoelessness.

sugyot.finalRuling: Going barefoot (without shoes) counts as a Yom Kippur affliction. The Gemara rejects two proposed proofs (David's barefoot ascent, which could describe a king without his horse and whip; Isaiah's barefoot walk, which could mean patched shoes) and derives it instead from Jeremiah's 'withhold your foot from being barefoot,' which casts bare feet as a hardship to be avoided.

display.whats: Deriving from Laban's words to Jacob that withholding conjugal relations is a Yom Kippur affliction
display.hint: From which verse does the Gemara derive that withholding conjugal relations counts as a Yom Kippur affliction?
display.title: Deriving the Affliction of Withholding Conjugal Relations

learning.ahaMoment: The Gemara does not treat withholding conjugal relations as an obviously implied affliction; it anchors the derivation in Laban's own words to Jacob, where 'if you shall afflict my daughters' names withholding marital relations as the very act of 'affliction.'
learning.memoryAnchor: Laban to Jacob: 'if you shall afflict my daughters' - that's the source for withheld conjugal relations as a Yom Kippur affliction.
learning.learnerQuestion: Where does the Gemara find a textual source for treating withheld conjugal relations as a Yom Kippur affliction?
learning.coreTension: Between treating marital withholding as an obviously implied affliction and the Gemara's insistence on anchoring it in a specific verse, here supplied by Laban's own choice of words.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara grounds the marital-relations affliction in Laban's own words to Jacob, reading 'if you shall afflict my daughters' as a warning against withholding conjugal relations from Leah and Rachel.

takeaway.text: Refraining from conjugal relations is a Yom Kippur affliction, derived from Laban's charge to Jacob that taking other wives would 'afflict' Leah and Rachel by withholding relations from them - the same verse-anchored method the Gemara applies to every one of the five afflictions.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume marital withholding is self-evidently an affliction and miss that the Gemara still requires - and finds - a specific verse naming it as such.

argumentFlow.label: Deriving that withholding marital relations is affliction
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishnah
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara turns to another Yom Kippur affliction and asks where the Torah calls refraining from conjugal relations 'inui.' It answers from Laban's words to Jacob, 'If you shall afflict my daughters,' which the Gemara understands as a warning against withholding marital relations.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners may think the Yom Kippur afflictions are an open list and that marital abstention is simply one obvious example.
misconceptions.correction: Each affliction needs a textual anchor. The Gemara specifically grounds marital abstention as 'inui' in Laban's words to Jacob, treating the derivation as necessary rather than self-evident.

quizSeeds.question: From which verse does the Gemara learn that withholding marital relations counts as 'inui'?
quizSeeds.answer: From Laban's charge to Jacob, 'If you shall afflict my daughters, and if you shall take other wives,' where 'afflict' is read as withholding conjugal relations from Leah and Rachel.

sugyot.finalRuling: Refraining from conjugal relations counts as a Yom Kippur affliction, derived from Laban's words to Jacob, 'If you shall afflict my daughters, and if you shall take other wives,' which the Gemara reads as identifying withholding marital relations as affliction.
